source.title: Exploring Grokking: Experimental and Mechanistic Investigations
source.authors: Qi-Ye Hu; Z. Hao; Ruo-Xi Yu

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Text extraction has minor garbling, but the relevant experimental descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs modular-addition grokking experiments, including experiments using the original code, and reports training and validation accuracy over training.
record.gate_note: The paper also summarizes mechanisms and findings from cited studies; those summaries are not this study's results. Figure 5 compares optimizer configurations, but the extracted text does not provide their plotted values.
record.test_reason: The study reruns modular addition (p=97) with the original Power et al. code and a simplified encoding. It reports training and validation accuracy over training across data fractions, the same method and measure as the original. It also extends the setup to MLP and LSTM models and to optimizer variants.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors report grokking in Transformers on mod-97 addition, most pronounced near a 50% training fraction, and say it matches Power et al. They do not observe grokking in MLP or LSTM, which they attribute to not using weight decay. Weight decay improves generalization most among the optimizer variants. They also say a harder encoding needs a larger training fraction.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses modular addition and reports running the original code, alongside a straightforward classification encoding. It also explores different architectures and optimization settings rather than only the original Transformer setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data fraction, encoding method, model architecture, and optimizer configuration affect the reported generalization behavior. The text reports no grokking at 15% in one Transformer setup, delayed generalization at 30%, and validation growth nearly concurrent with training at higher fractions; it also reports no grokking for the tested MLP and LSTM.

fits_no_version.finding: Within an 1800-update budget, AdamW with weight decay 1 gives the most generalization among the optimizer variants. Some generalization occurs without weight decay at high data fractions, and suboptimal hyperparameters severely limit it (Figure 5 caption).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay accelerates generalization on modular addition within a fixed budget, relative to other optimizer and noise interventions.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2022 is printed in the text; the supplied study metadata identifies the venue as arXiv.org.
record.problems: Some results are described only qualitatively or appear in figures without extracted values. The paper does not report uncertainty estimates. Its optimizer-configuration text and Figure 5h label do not align clearly. The conclusion that delay grows as training data shrinks is not established across the tested fractions.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted from the extracted text. Figure 5 values are recorded as figure only because the text does not provide their plotted values.

untested.parts: No quantitative delay-versus-fraction relationship is stated in the text; Figure 7 (steps until generalization) is figure only. No seeds or uncertainty are reported.
No circuit analysis or progress measures.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm sweep. Omnigrok is only cited.
Weight decay is varied only within an 1800-step budget. There is no critical dataset size, ungrokking or efficiency measure.
Optimizer variants are not analysed as causes of the delay, and there are no floating-point controls.

missing.what: Original-code runs at small fractions (5%, 30%): validation accuracy does not grow until the fraction reaches about 40%.
Encoding comparison: both encodings grok, but the official encoding needs a larger training fraction to generalize.
Steps until generalization versus training fraction (figure only), plus MLP validation loss rising late in training.

record.verdict_notes: This is a student-style report. The NeurIPS 2022 header looks like a template artifact rather than peer review. It has a single run per condition and no uncertainty reported. Section 5 summarizes cited work (Liu et al., Lyu et al.) and contains no results of its own. Figure 5's caption order and the text's variant list disagree on learning rates and on panel h (full batch versus minibatch 128).

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not establish a general quantitative relationship between training-set size and delay across all tested fractions; one very small fraction fails to generalize within the reported run.
No gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, or continuous progress measure is measured in the study's experiments.
Experiments use algorithmic modular addition, not non-algorithmic data; the study does not sweep initialization scale or weight norm or test a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
Weight decay is varied, but the study does not test circuit efficiency, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.
The study does not identify or compare learned algorithms across runs.
Optimizer settings are compared, but adaptive-optimizer instabilities and floating-point softmax limits are not controlled or tested as causes of the delay.

relationships.reason: Training accuracy saturates early (about 200 steps at 30%) and validation jumps much later (about 6k–9.1k steps, or about 6000 epochs) (R2, R3, R4, R5).
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy saturated around step 200 at a 30% training fraction, while validation jumped much later, around 6,000–9,100 steps or 6,000 epochs across the tested setups.
